title: Tool design
summary: Design tool contracts that let an agent distinguish evidence, absence, and failure before it acts.
overview: A tool is an executable interface the model can request: an operation with documented inputs, results, and errors. The application executes it. MCP, the Model Context Protocol, specifies one way to expose these interfaces. A valid response shape does not establish that the underlying data is complete or correct.
why: During manual incident triage, an engineer notices a failed dashboard request and investigates. When an agent receives only the adapter’s output, that distinction must survive the interface. Returning an empty list after a timeout can turn missing evidence into a confident claim that nothing happened. Start with one read-only workflow before delegating operational changes.
example: An engineer asks whether payments had incidents during the last hour. Propose search_incidents(service, start_time, end_time, limit, cursor). Return incident IDs, short summaries, the searched interval, and a continuation cursor. A completed empty search returns status=ok with items=[]; a backend timeout returns status=error with code=TIMEOUT. These are illustrative application fields, not mandatory MCP fields. With MCP, report execution failure using isError=true. A client-side transport timeout may produce no tool result at all; the caller must preserve that failure too.
judgment: Choose granularity around a useful task and its failure boundaries. Searching and fetching one incident can be separate; searching, deciding, and closing an incident should not be one opaque action. Keep IDs for follow-up reads. Evaluate concise output without omitting uncertainty, pagination, or evidence.
next: Can your agent distinguish a complete empty search, a partial result, and a failed lookup in recorded runs, without help from a person reading backend logs?

JSON Schema: Object properties and validation
AWS Builders’ Library: Timeouts, retries, and backoff with jitter

learning.relevance: Teams adopting agents already know API design, but now a model selects operations and interprets their results. Making uncertainty explicit gives the team a small, observable improvement to implement before expanding autonomy.
outcomes: Specify a bounded incident-search interface with useful follow-up identifiers.
Demonstrate separate successful-empty, partial, and execution-error results.
Evaluate the agent’s conclusion and enforce a retry budget in application code.

workflow.before: An engineer searches dashboards, notices failed requests, reads incident records, and writes a triage note.
workflow.after: An agent requests a bounded search, fetches relevant records, and drafts a note citing the returned IDs and unresolved gaps.
workflow.human: The engineer defines access and retry policies, checks evidence, and owns incident decisions and production changes.

walkthrough: 1. Write the decision first: identify incidents for payments within an explicit UTC interval. Define inclusive start and exclusive end, a maximum result count, and what a continuation cursor means. State that this operation reads records and does not close incidents. These choices are a proposed team contract.

2. Validate arguments before the backend call. JSON Schema properties alone do not make fields required or forbid extra keys; declare those constraints deliberately. Validate the interval and authorize the caller against the requested service in server code. Tool names, descriptions, annotations, and persistent prompts are not access controls.

3. Preserve what happened. Return successful empty results only after the specified search completed. Expose more available results through a cursor; if coverage is incomplete, return that limitation explicitly. Model a timeout as an error, not an empty collection. Publish and validate structured results where your integration supports them. A result-count limit does not bound bytes or tokens when individual records are large; cap or summarize record fields and expose any omitted coverage.

4. Define the next safe action outside the model. For this read-only exercise, allow one delayed retry for a transient timeout; otherwise report the lookup as unresolved. The application counts attempts. Production policies should account for backend load, deadlines, backoff, and jitter; retrying writes additionally requires safe side-effect handling.

5. Inspect recorded requests, responses, and final answers across repeated runs. Compare whether the agent reports uncertainty and cites real records, then assess tool calls and output size. A cleaner schema is a hypothesis until the task outcomes improve; successful retrieval still does not establish an incident’s root cause.
pitfalls: Catching every exception and returning [] hides an outage as a clean search.
Dropping pagination or coverage fields makes a short result look exhaustive.
Relying on a retry hint in text leaves the actual call budget unenforced.
Treating an incident summary as an instruction lets retrieved text steer actions.

exercise.title: Make an incident lookup fail honestly
steps: Stub four responses: one incident, completed empty, partial results, and timeout.
Add argument validation, explicit outcomes, and an application-enforced retry limit.
Run the same triage request against each fixture several times; capture calls and answers.
Review incorrect conclusions with a teammate and revise the contract or caller.
success: Timeout and partial fixtures never produce an unqualified “no incidents” conclusion in the recorded runs.
Successful answers cite fixture IDs; the timeout case stays within the configured attempt budget.
Invalid intervals and unauthorized service requests are rejected before backend execution.
